analysis.one_liner: Makes producers pay to collect and recycle their packaging and bans many single-use plastic products.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing, a markup, or a vote: referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee on June 11, 2020, it sat there with zero cosponsors until the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would shift the cost of managing America's packaging waste from taxpayers and local governments to the companies that make the products. Producers would have to fund collection, recycling, and composting of their packaging, pay a 10-cent minimum refund on beverage containers, and put clear recyclable-or-not labels on products. It would ban single-use plastic carryout bags and plastic utensils, limit plastic straws to on-request, phase out other throwaway plastic items, require recycled content in plastic bottles, cap exports of plastic waste to other countries, and temporarily block new or expanded permits for plastics manufacturing plants until pollution rules catch up.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people benefit most: communities near plastic-polluted waterways and landfills, households that would get refunds for returning containers and free producer-funded recycling collection, and local governments, whose waste-management and litter-cleanup bills would be paid by producers instead of taxpayers. Recycling and composting businesses would gain a large new stream of producer-funded investment.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Households and local taxpayers; the recycling industry

how_it_helps.text: Makes producers of packaging, paper, single-use products, and beverage containers fiscally responsible for collecting, managing, and recycling or composting them after consumer use.
Creates a national beverage container deposit program with a refund of at least 10 cents per container, redeemable at retailers or redemption centers open at least 10 hours a day.

Bans single-use plastic carryout bags at retail, bans plastic utensils, limits plastic straws to customers who request them, and directs phase-outs of other non-recyclable single-use items such as foam food service products and hotel mini toiletry bottles.
Places a temporary moratorium on new or expanded permits for facilities that manufacture plastics until regulations are updated to address pollution from those facilities.
Requires minimum post-consumer recycled content in plastic beverage containers, starting at 25 percent by 2025 and rising to 80 percent by 2040.
Establishes limitations on the export of plastic waste to other countries and requires programs to track and publicly report where collected materials actually go.
Prohibits charging covered households and public spaces any amount for producer-funded collection, so recycling stays free at the point of use.

analysis.who_pays: Plastic resin, packaging, and beverage companies pay the fees, deposits, recycled-content, and redesign requirements, and larger retailers and restaurants bear compliance duties for bag, utensil, and container-return rules; some of these costs would likely be passed through to consumers in prices. Businesses with under $1 million in annual revenue are exempt.

drawbacks.text: Producer fees and compliance costs would likely be passed through to consumers as modestly higher prices for packaged goods and beverages; the bill sets the fee structure but cannot cap what companies charge at the shelf.

The beverage deposit is an upfront cash outlay for shoppers until they return the container, and retailers must handle returns with daily caps (250 containers per person per day at large stores, 50 at small ones).

Producer Responsibility Organizations are exempt from antitrust laws when carrying out an approved plan, which lets competing brands coordinate fees and programs without the usual competition-law limits.

The moratorium on new or expanded plastics manufacturing permits would delay facility investment and capacity until EPA updates its pollution regulations, which industry argued constrains production during the wait.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is a fair one on its face: waste costs move from local taxpayers to the companies that design and profit from the packaging, with household price effects likely small and small businesses exempt. The design has real warts: the antitrust exemption for industry-run producer organizations invites coordination problems, the deposit program shifts handling burdens to retailers and cash-flow burdens to shoppers, and enforcement rests heavily on EPA rule-writing that could be slow or weakened. Still, an honest weighing finds the public benefits, cleaner waterways and a functioning domestic recycling system, larger than the costs, which is presumably why the industries affected worked to make sure it never moved.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which never held a hearing or markup, and it expired with the Congress in January 2021 without a single cosponsor or vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Tom Udall introduced the bill on June 11, 2020, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works the same day.
No cosponsors ever signed on in the Senate.
The committee took no further action, and there is no hearing, markup, or vote of any kind in the bill's action history before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Plastic resin, packaging, and beverage manufacturers came out ahead: they continue to pay nothing for the waste their products generate, state and local governments keep bearing those cleanup and recycling costs, and no permit moratorium or recycled-content mandate constrains them. Taxpayers and communities near plastic-polluted waterways gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Plastic and beverage makers; taxpayers keep the cost

for.name: Sen. Tom Udall
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and served as its only Senate sponsor; no colleague joined him.

for.name: Environmental and public-health organizations
for.what_they_did: Publicly backed the bill and its House companion, championing producer responsibility and the plastics-permit moratorium as the most comprehensive federal plastic-pollution proposal of the Congress.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action on it, no hearing, no markup, no report, for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: Sen. John Barrasso
against.role: Chair, Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: As the chairman who controlled the committee's agenda, never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup, keeping it off the floor entirely.

against.name: Petrochemical and plastics industry
against.role: Chemical manufacturers and packaging trade associations
against.what_they_did: Opposed extended producer responsibility, recycled-content mandates, and the moratorium on new plastics-plant permits, arguing they would raise costs; the permit moratorium in particular drew industry opposition.

against.name: Beverage and packaging companies
against.role: Coca-Cola, PepsiCo, and packaging trade groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed the national bottle-deposit program and producer-fee structure, which would have made them directly responsible for container and packaging waste and cut into profits from new plastic production.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party; the Republican-chaired committee it went to never acted on it, and no vote was ever taken that could have crossed party lines.

industries.note: The bill imposes producer fees for waste collection, a recycled-content mandate, design and labeling rules, product bans, and a temporary moratorium on new or expanded plastics-plant permits until pollution rules are updated. It also excludes chemical conversion methods like pyrolysis and gasification from the definition of recycling, which would block the industry's preferred loophole. Ordinary people pay less for waste management; this industry pays more.

Beverage producers would collect 10-cent minimum deposits, fund the redemption system, and meet rising recycled-content requirements for plastic bottles (25 percent by 2025 rising to 80 percent by 2040). The deposit money from unreturned containers must be invested in collection and recycling infrastructure rather than kept as profit.

Larger retailers and restaurants must stop handing out single-use plastic bags and utensils, dispense straws only on request, and accept container returns with daily caps. Businesses under $1 million in annual revenue are exempt, and many chains already comply with similar state laws; consumers get cleaner service at the counter.

Producer-funded programs must spend at least half of their first ten years of expenditures building and upgrading U.S. recycling and composting infrastructure, and pay collection and redemption services fully for their costs. This is a large, durable new revenue stream financed by packaging producers.

The bill requires producers, not local taxpayers, to cover the management and cleanup costs local governments currently absorb, and requires an annual report on the resulting reductions in state and local taxes. Municipalities also gain a voice on industry advisory committees.
